claims.text: The local catalog models the Quick Starter Gift Set Red Deck as released on December 4, 1998, as a child lane inside the Quick Starter Gift Set product.
Bulbapedia describes Quick Starter Gift Set as a two-deck kit containing a Red Deck and a Green Deck.
The local Red Deck catalog models one 60-card deck with 32 unique catalog rows; the parent rollup preserves the red lane rather than deduplicating by card name.
Bulbapedia frames Quick Starter cards as reprints from Vending Machine / Expansion Sheet material, while the local catalog preserves the Red Deck as a child lane with its own row order.
The local symbol-status matrix marks the Quick Starter parent product as printing without rarity symbols and identifies Base-overlap trainer traps, including Gust of Wind and Switch.
Lower-tier collector research warns that Quick Starter trainer reprints without rarity symbols can be mistaken for Japanese Base No Rarity cards when the agent only checks a missing corner symbol.
The local Red Deck attention rows include Squirtle, two Pikachu rows, Raichu, Zapdos, Gust of Wind, and Switch.
The local Red Deck artist clusters include Atsuko Nishida, Keiji Kinebuchi, Kagemaru Himeno, Ken Sugimori, Naoyo Kimura, Tomokazu Komiya, and others.

The Red Deck matters because it turns Quick Starter into a lightning-and-water teaching lane: Squirtle opens one friendly door, Pikachu appears twice, Raichu and Zapdos raise the voltage, and the trainer rows quietly teach why missing-symbol resemblance is not provenance.

special_identification_instructions.trigger: A listing, want, scan, or agent memory says Quick Starter Red Deck, red deck, QSGSR, Red Green Gift Set, no-rarity deck card, old-back Pikachu, old-back Squirtle, or missing-symbol trainer.
special_identification_instructions.summary: The Red Deck is a child lane inside Quick Starter Gift Set; preserve the lane, row order, and missing-symbol trap context.
steps: Preserve release_family_id jp_tcg_quick_starter_gift_set_red_deck_19981204 when the evidence points to the Red Deck child catalog.
Do not collapse the Red Deck into the Quick Starter parent rollup unless the parent/child distinction is explicitly preserved.
Do not treat lack of a rarity symbol as Japanese Base No Rarity proof; Quick Starter is a separate missing-symbol source.
For duplicate names, especially Pikachu, require row-level image or text evidence before moving from catalog match to identification confidence.
For trainer overlap rows, require Japanese text/layout comparison against known Expansion Pack and Quick Starter exemplars.

narrative.human_title: The red half of the lesson
narrative.why_it_matters: The Red Deck is Quick Starter with the lights on. It starts soft with Squirtle, then lets Pikachu appear twice, then lets Raichu and Zapdos make the deck feel charged. That is the fun part. The serious part is stranger: the same product that feels like a beginner bridge is also one of the best traps for a careless No Rarity search. A missing symbol can be visible and still point to the wrong assembly history.

narrative.human_title: A water starter at the red door
narrative.why_it_matters: Squirtle 001 gives the Red Deck a gentle first handshake. Before the duplicate Pikachu rows and the legendary-bird voltage, the deck begins with a starter a kid already knows how to love. Himeno's credit gives the row a softer visual register, and the catalog job is simple: keep that red-deck doorway from dissolving into generic Squirtle memory.

narrative.human_title: The mascot row that still needs a row number
narrative.why_it_matters: Pikachu 009 is warm in the obvious way: Atsuko Nishida, the mascot, the face a collector sees before reading a line of provenance. But the Red Deck makes that warmth dangerous if an agent gets lazy. There is another Pikachu beside it. The charm begins with the character; the identification begins with the row.

narrative.human_title: The second Pikachu is the lesson
narrative.why_it_matters: Pikachu 010 proves the Red Deck is not searchable by affection alone. Sugimori's credit pulls the row toward the official design memory of Pokemon, but its real protocol value is sharper: same character, same product lane, adjacent row, different evidence needs. The agent has to slow down.

narrative.human_title: The red deck lets Pikachu grow up
narrative.why_it_matters: Raichu gives the Red Deck a little arc. Pikachu is not only a face here; it is a line with weight and movement. Nishida's credit keeps the evolution close to Pokemon's creature-design origins, while the Quick Starter context keeps it practical: this is wonder built for someone actually learning to play.

narrative.why_it_matters: Zapdos makes the Quick Starter Red Deck feel charged. It is a beginner product, yes, but it still gives the player a legendary bird to look at and imagine around. Kimura's credit belongs to that quieter early-Pokemon texture where a card can be both practical and mythic.

narrative.human_title: A useful trainer with a dangerous blank corner
narrative.why_it_matters: Gust of Wind is exactly the sort of card a collector-agent should be humble around. It is playable language, early trainer memory, and a missing-symbol trap all at once. The row asks the protocol's favorite question in cardboard form: does this thing merely resemble the route, or can it prove the route?

narrative.human_title: The tiny trainer that can switch the whole route
narrative.why_it_matters: Switch is plain until it is not. In a binder it can look like low-drama trainer cardboard; in the protocol it is a provenance hinge. If the agent only sees an empty rarity corner, it may walk straight into the wrong family. If it asks for text and layout, the card becomes legible without pretending to be proven.
